cluster.name: Kedarnath
cluster.summary: A high-Himalayan pilgrimage circuit centred on the Kedarnath temple at 3,583 m, reached by a 16 km trek from Gaurikund. The shrine opens only from roughly late April to early November; everything else in this cluster is planned around that window and around genuine altitude and weather risk.
cluster.intercity_hub: Jolly Grant Airport, Dehradun (DED) / Rishikesh road head, 8-10 hours to Sonprayag
cluster.source_title: Shri Badarinath Shri Kedarnath Temple Committee

attractions.name: Kedarnath Temple
attractions.summary: One of the twelve jyotirlingas, standing at 3,583 m below the Kedarnath peak, open only for about six months a year.
attractions.history: The temple in its present stone form is traditionally attributed to Adi Shankaracharya in the eighth century CE, rebuilding on a site associated with the Pandavas. It is constructed of interlocking grey stone slabs without mortar, which is why it survived the catastrophic 2013 Kedarnath floods largely intact while the settlement around it was destroyed - a large boulder diverted the debris flow around the structure.
attractions.significance: Kedarnath is the highest of the twelve jyotirlingas and one of the four Chota Char Dham shrines of Uttarakhand, along with Badrinath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. The lingam here is worshipped in an irregular conical rock form rather than a carved lingam. The temple closes for winter on Bhai Dooj, when the deity is carried to Ukhimath for six months.
interesting_facts: The temple is built of interlocking stone slabs with no mortar.
A boulder now known as Bhim Shila diverted the 2013 flood debris around the temple.
The deity is moved to Omkareshwar Temple at Ukhimath for the winter months.
Opening and closing dates are announced each year on Maha Shivaratri, based on the Hindu calendar.
attractions.accessibility_notes: At 3,583 m and reached only by a 16 km trek, helicopter or pony. The temple platform has steps. Altitude sickness is a serious and common risk. Anyone with heart, lung or blood-pressure conditions should obtain medical advice before attempting the journey; mandatory health screening applies at the registration point.
attractions.dress_code: Modest traditional dress plus genuine cold-weather clothing - temperatures fall below freezing even in season. Footwear removed at the temple.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography inside the temple is strictly prohibited. Mobile phones must generally be deposited or switched off.
local_customs: Char Dham registration is mandatory and must be completed before travelling.
Ascend over two days if possible; do not attempt Gaurikund to Kedarnath and back in one day.
Carry your own medication; medical posts along the route are basic.
The route closes at short notice for weather; build spare days into the plan.
Do not litter - waste removal from the valley is extremely difficult.

schedule.note: Darshan windows with a midday break; open only when the shrine is in season
Closed from Bhai Dooj to Akshaya Tritiya; deity moved to Ukhimath

costs.note: Darshan is free; special darshan passes may be available
Optional helicopter return from Phata/Sersi/Guptkashi, booked via the official IRCTC heliyatra portal

attractions.verification_note: Opening dates are announced annually on Maha Shivaratri. Registration, helicopter booking and route status change every season - verify on the official portals before travelling.

sources.title: Shri Badarinath Shri Kedarnath Temple Committee - official

attractions.name: Gaurikund-Kedarnath Trek
attractions.summary: The 16 km paved pilgrim route climbing about 1,600 m from Gaurikund to the shrine, rebuilt after the 2013 floods.
attractions.history: The traditional pilgrim route was destroyed in the June 2013 floods, which killed thousands along this valley. It was rebuilt on a realigned, wider and better-engineered alignment with rest shelters, medical posts and improved drainage. The new route is longer than the old one but substantially safer.
attractions.significance: The trek is the pilgrimage itself for most who undertake it - the physical effort of the ascent is understood as part of the devotional act. It is also the clearest illustration of post-disaster reconstruction in the Indian Himalaya, with the rebuilt route designed explicitly for flood resilience.
interesting_facts: The route climbs roughly 1,600 m over 16 km.
Ponies, palanquins (pithoo/dandi) and porters are available at regulated rates.
Rest shelters and medical posts are spaced along the rebuilt route.
Most walkers take six to nine hours up and four to six hours down.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A sustained 1,600 m ascent at altitude. Not accessible. Pony and palanquin services exist at regulated rates and are the only realistic option for those who cannot walk it, but even these involve exposure to cold and altitude.
attractions.dress_code: Layered warm clothing, waterproof outer layer, broken-in trekking shoes, sun protection. Weather changes within minutes.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted along the route.
local_customs: Start before 05:00 to reach Kedarnath in daylight.
Use only registered pony and porter services at the posted rates.
Drink water constantly; altitude dehydration is rapid.
Turn back if you develop headache, nausea or breathlessness that does not resolve.
Carry all waste back down.

schedule.note: Last permitted start time for the ascent is enforced
Route closed outside the shrine season

costs.note: Pony or palanquin one way, at regulated rates

attractions.verification_note: Route status, last-start times and regulated pony rates are set each season and change with weather - verify with the district administration before setting out.

attractions.name: Bhairavnath Temple, Kedarnath
attractions.summary: A small shrine on the ridge above Kedarnath, guardian of the valley, with the best view back over the main temple.
attractions.history: Bhairav is regarded as the guardian deity of Kedarnath, and tradition holds that he protects the valley through the six winter months when the main temple is closed and the settlement is abandoned. The shrine sits about a kilometre above and south of the temple.
attractions.significance: Visiting Bhairavnath is customarily considered to complete the Kedarnath darshan. The short climb also gives the clearest overview of the temple against the Kedarnath and Kharchkund peaks, and of the 2013 debris field.
interesting_facts: Bhairav is believed to guard the valley during the winter closure.
The climb takes roughly thirty to forty-five minutes from the main temple.
The vantage point shows the path the 2013 debris flow took around the temple.
Many pilgrims skip it, so it is far quieter than the main shrine.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A steep, exposed climb of roughly a kilometre at 3,600 m with no railing. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Warm layers and windproof outer; the ridge is exposed.
local_customs: Do not attempt in poor visibility - the path is exposed.
Go in the morning; afternoon weather closes in quickly.
attractions.verification_note: Access depends entirely on weather and snow cover - verify locally.

sources.title: Shri Badarinath Shri Kedarnath Temple Committee

attractions.name: Gaurikund
attractions.summary: The road head and trailhead for Kedarnath at 1,982 m, with a hot spring and the temple to Gauri.
attractions.history: Gaurikund is named for Parvati (Gauri), who according to tradition performed austerities here to win Shiva. A natural thermal spring feeds bathing tanks used by pilgrims before beginning the ascent. The settlement was severely damaged in the 2013 floods and has been partially rebuilt.
attractions.significance: Gaurikund is the last road-accessible point on the Kedarnath route and therefore the operational hub of the yatra: registration checks, pony stands, porters, medical screening and the final supply point before the trek.
interesting_facts: The natural hot spring is fed by geothermal activity beneath the valley.
It sits at 1,982 m, about 1,600 m below the shrine.
Private vehicles stop at Sonprayag; shared jeeps cover the last stretch to Gaurikund.
The 2013 floods destroyed much of the settlement, including part of the hot spring complex.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The settlement is built on a steep slope with stepped lanes throughout. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress; warm layers. Separate bathing areas for men and women at the spring.
attractions.photography_policy: Do not photograph people bathing at the hot spring.
local_customs: Char Dham registration is verified here - carry your documents.
Pony and porter rates are regulated and posted; do not pay above them.
Accommodation is basic and fills early in season.

schedule.note: Largely closed outside the yatra season

costs.note: Free; hot-spring bathing may carry a nominal charge

attractions.verification_note: Facilities and access change every season after monsoon damage - verify before travelling.

attractions.name: Triyuginarayan Temple
attractions.summary: The temple where Shiva and Parvati are believed to have married, before an eternal flame said to have burned for three ages.
attractions.history: Tradition holds that Shiva and Parvati were married at this spot with Vishnu presiding, and that the fire lit for the ceremony has burned continuously ever since - hence 'Triyugi', three ages. The temple's architecture resembles Kedarnath's and is also attributed to the period of Adi Shankaracharya.
attractions.significance: Triyuginarayan is one of the few Himalayan temples where the central ritual object is a perpetual fire rather than an image, and pilgrims traditionally carry wood as an offering. It has become a sought-after wedding venue for couples seeking to marry at the mythological site of Shiva's own marriage.
interesting_facts: The havan fire is said to have burned continuously across three yugas.
Pilgrims traditionally offer wood to the fire rather than flowers.
Ash from the fire is taken as prasad.
Four kunds (water tanks) around the temple are associated with the wedding rituals.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The road reaches the village but the temple is approached by steps. The mountain road is narrow and winding.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress; warm layers. Footwear removed at the temple.
attractions.photography_policy: Ask before photographing the fire or rituals.
local_customs: Offering wood to the fire is the customary practice.
Do not extinguish or disturb the flame.
Weddings are frequently held here - be unobtrusive if one is in progress.
attractions.verification_note: Road access can be cut by landslides - verify before travelling.

attractions.name: Guptkashi & Vishwanath Temple
attractions.summary: A hillside town at 1,319 m with an ancient Vishwanath temple, the standard acclimatisation stop before Kedarnath.
attractions.history: The name means 'hidden Kashi', from the tradition that Shiva concealed himself here while avoiding the Pandavas before reappearing at Kedarnath. The Vishwanath temple mirrors its Varanasi namesake, and the adjacent Manikarnik Kund receives water from two spouts representing the Ganga and Yamuna.
attractions.significance: Guptkashi is the practical base of the Kedarnath yatra: it has the best accommodation on the route, sits at a sensible acclimatisation altitude, and is the departure point for several helicopter services. Its temple complex is a significant pilgrimage site independent of Kedarnath.
interesting_facts: The name means 'hidden Kashi'.
Water flows into the Manikarnik Kund from two spouts representing the Ganga and Yamuna.
It is the recommended overnight stop for acclimatisation before the Kedarnath ascent.
The town has a clear view of the Chaukhamba massif in good weather.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The town is on a slope with stepped lanes; the temple courtyard is reached by steps but the road passes close.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed at the temple.
local_customs: Spend a night here to acclimatise before ascending - this materially reduces altitude sickness risk.
Accommodation fills quickly in season; book ahead.
attractions.verification_note: Timings are not formally published - verify locally.

attractions.name: Omkareshwar Temple, Ukhimath
attractions.summary: The winter seat of Kedarnath: the deity is carried here each November and worshipped until the shrine reopens in spring.
attractions.history: Ukhimath at 1,311 m has served as the winter seat of the Kedarnath deity for centuries. When the high shrine closes on Bhai Dooj the palanquin is carried down over several days and installed here, where daily worship continues through the winter. The temple is also associated with the marriage of Usha and Aniruddha in local tradition.
attractions.significance: Ukhimath is the only place where Kedarnath worship continues year-round, which makes it the practical alternative for pilgrims travelling outside the six-month shrine season. The transfer procession itself is a significant ritual event in the valley.
interesting_facts: Kedarnath's deity is worshipped here for roughly six months each year.
The palanquin procession from Kedarnath takes several days and passes through village halts.
The Madhyamaheshwar deity also winters here.
It is the correct destination for anyone visiting the region between November and April.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The temple courtyard is reached by a flight of steps from the road; the courtyard itself is level.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress; warm layers in winter. Footwear removed at the entrance.
local_customs: This is the correct place to seek Kedarnath darshan outside the shrine season.
Winter temperatures here are low - dress accordingly.
attractions.verification_note: Timings and procession dates change annually - verify with the temple committee.

sources.title: Shri Badarinath Shri Kedarnath Temple Committee

attractions.name: Chopta & Tungnath Temple
attractions.summary: The world's highest Shiva temple at 3,680 m, reached by a 3.5 km trek from Chopta's rhododendron meadows.
attractions.history: Tungnath is one of the Panch Kedar, the five temples where parts of Shiva's bull form are said to have surfaced - the arms at Tungnath. The temple is traditionally over a thousand years old. Chandrashila, the summit a further kilometre above, is associated with Rama's meditation after the Lanka campaign.
attractions.significance: Tungnath is the highest Shiva temple in the world and the most accessible of the Panch Kedar. The Chopta-Tungnath-Chandrashila route is among the few Himalayan treks that a reasonably fit beginner can complete in a day, with a summit panorama covering Nanda Devi, Trishul, Kedar and Chaukhamba.
interesting_facts: At 3,680 m it is the highest Shiva temple in the world.
It is one of the Panch Kedar, where Shiva's arms are said to have appeared.
The Chandrashila summit a kilometre further up reaches about 4,000 m.
Chopta's meadows turn red with rhododendron bloom in April and May.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A 3.5 km paved but steep ascent gaining roughly 700 m, at altitude. Not accessible. Snow covers the route from December to March.
attractions.dress_code: Layered warm clothing, windproof shell, trekking shoes. Temperatures at the summit are far below those at Chopta.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography permitted outdoors; sanctum photography is not.
local_customs: Start early; afternoon cloud closes the summit view.
The temple closes for winter like Kedarnath, with the deity moved to Mukkumath.
Carry water - there is no reliable source on the ascent.
Do not litter on the meadow.

schedule.note: Temple closed; deity moved to Mukkumath

costs.note: Free temple entry; forest entry charge may apply

attractions.verification_note: Snow closes the route without notice from late autumn - verify conditions locally.

attractions.name: Deoria Tal
attractions.summary: A small emerald lake at 2,438 m that reflects the Chaukhamba massif, reached by a 2.5 km climb from Sari village.
attractions.history: Deoria Tal - 'lake of the gods' - is associated in the Mahabharata tradition with the Yaksha Prashna, the riddle contest in which a spirit questioned the Pandavas at a lake before allowing them to drink. The trail from Sari village was formalised for visitors in recent decades.
attractions.significance: The lake is the single best short walk in the Kedarnath region: two hours of climbing gives a mirror reflection of Chaukhamba, Nilkantha and the Bandarpunch range in still morning water. It is also a popular first camping location for those acclimatising before higher treks.
interesting_facts: The reflection is sharpest in the first hour after sunrise, before wind ruffles the surface.
The lake is linked to the Yaksha Prashna episode of the Mahabharata.
Camping is permitted at designated spots with a forest permit.
The climb from Sari is roughly 2.5 km and gains about 400 m.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A 2.5 km stone-stepped climb gaining about 400 m. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Warm layers, trekking shoes, rain shell.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; drones require forest permission.
local_customs: Camping requires a forest department permit obtained at Sari.
Do not wash or bathe in the lake.
Carry all waste back down.

schedule.note: Day access; camping needs a permit

attractions.verification_note: Forest permit rules and camping availability change - verify at Sari before setting out.

attractions.name: Sonprayag
attractions.summary: The confluence of the Mandakini and Basuki rivers at 1,829 m, and the vehicle terminus for the Kedarnath yatra.
attractions.history: Sonprayag is one of the sacred confluences of the Garhwal Himalaya, where the Basuki joins the Mandakini. It functions as the mandatory vehicle stop for the Kedarnath route: private vehicles park here and shared jeeps carry pilgrims the final 5 km to Gaurikund. Biometric registration verification also takes place here.
attractions.significance: As the gateway checkpoint for Kedarnath, Sonprayag is where the administrative machinery of the yatra is most visible - registration, medical screening, crowd management and weather-based route control all run from here.
interesting_facts: Private vehicles cannot proceed beyond Sonprayag; shared jeeps cover the last 5 km.
Char Dham registration is verified at the checkpoint here.
It sits at the Mandakini-Basuki confluence, itself a sacred site.
The road beyond is frequently closed for weather; the decision is taken here.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Steep stepped lanes and a crowded transport terminus. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Warm layers; the confluence is windy.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; do not photograph the security checkpoint.
local_customs: Carry printed Char Dham registration and photo identity.
Shared jeep fares to Gaurikund are fixed - do not pay above the posted rate.
Parking fills before dawn in peak season.

schedule.note: Route beyond largely closed outside the yatra season

attractions.verification_note: Registration rules, fares and route control change every season - verify before travelling.

attractions.name: Rudraprayag Sangam
attractions.summary: The confluence of the Alaknanda and Mandakini, second of the Panch Prayag, with a viewing platform at the meeting point.
attractions.history: Rudraprayag is one of the Panch Prayag, the five sacred confluences of the Alaknanda system. Tradition associates it with Shiva appearing in his Rudra form to the sage Narada. The town is also known for the man-eating leopard of Rudraprayag, hunted by Jim Corbett in 1926.
attractions.significance: The Panch Prayag confluences are ritually essential stops on the Char Dham route, and Rudraprayag is where the Kedarnath valley's river joins the main Alaknanda. The colour difference between the two rivers is clearly visible at the meeting point.
interesting_facts: It is the second of the five Panch Prayag confluences.
The two rivers have visibly different colours where they meet.
Jim Corbett shot the man-eating leopard of Rudraprayag near here in 1926.
A stepped platform allows visitors to reach the water at the confluence.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The confluence platform is reached by a long flight of steps from the road.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; avoid photographing bathers.
local_customs: The current at the confluence is strong - do not enter deep water.
Ritual bathing is common; be respectful of those performing rites.
attractions.verification_note: Free open site; water levels vary sharply with season.

attractions.name: Vasuki Tal
attractions.summary: A glacial lake at 4,135 m about 8 km above Kedarnath, with views of the Chaukhamba peaks. Serious high-altitude trekking only.
attractions.history: Vasuki Tal lies above the Kedarnath basin, fed by the Chaturangi and Vasuki glaciers. Tradition holds that Vishnu bathed here on Raksha Bandhan. The route from Kedarnath climbs steeply past Chorabari Tal and onto exposed moraine.
attractions.significance: Vasuki Tal is the highest point most trekkers in this valley reach, and one of the few places where the glacial systems feeding the Mandakini are directly visible. Brahma Kamal, the Himalayan state flower of Uttarakhand, grows along the upper route.
interesting_facts: The lake sits at 4,135 m, roughly 550 m above Kedarnath.
Brahma Kamal, Uttarakhand's state flower, grows on the upper slopes.
The route crosses unstable moraine and requires a guide.
Snow can persist on the approach well into June.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A steep 8 km climb from 3,583 m to 4,135 m over loose moraine, at altitude where acute mountain sickness is a real risk. For experienced high-altitude trekkers with a guide only.
attractions.dress_code: Full high-altitude kit: insulated layers, windproof shell, gloves, sun protection, proper boots.
local_customs: A local guide is essential; the route is not marked throughout.
Inform the local administration before setting out.
Turn back at any sign of altitude sickness.
Do not attempt as a day trip without prior acclimatisation at Kedarnath.
attractions.verification_note: Route conditions vary year to year and permission may be required - verify with the local administration and a registered guide before attempting.
